note:
Dermatology follow-up on the hospital ward for a 27-year-old male who is hospitalized for an unrelated orthopedic problem and asked for help with his facial skin. He reports pimples on his face and upper back for about three years that have worsened over the past two months, with tender bumps along the jawline. He has used an over-the-counter face wash intermittently without lasting benefit. He denies fever, denies itching, and denies any drainage from the lesions. He has no other chronic medical conditions and is not using any acne treatment at this time.

On examination he is comfortable and afebrile. There are multiple open and closed comedones across the forehead and cheeks, along with scattered inflammatory papules and a few pustules on the cheeks and jawline. There are no nodules or cysts, and no significant scarring. The upper back shows a few similar papules. The rest of the skin examination is unremarkable.

Impression is mild to moderate acne vulgaris, predominantly comedonal with some inflammatory lesions. I explained that this is unrelated to his hospital stay and that treatment takes eight to twelve weeks to show its full effect. I started adapalene 0.1% gel to be applied to the face every night at bedtime and benzoyl peroxide 5% gel to be applied each morning. He was advised to use a gentle cleanser and a non-comedogenic moisturizer, to avoid picking at the lesions, and to expect some dryness during the first two weeks. He will follow up in dermatology clinic eight weeks after discharge, and an oral antibiotic can be considered if the response is inadequate.
summary: A 27-year-old male hospitalized for an unrelated orthopedic problem was seen by dermatology for pimples on the face and upper back that have worsened over the past two months. He denies fever, itching and drainage, and examination showed comedones, inflammatory papules and a few pustules without nodules, cysts or significant scarring. The impression is mild to moderate acne vulgaris. Adapalene 0.1% gel at bedtime and benzoyl peroxide 5% gel each morning were started with skin care advice, and he will follow up in dermatology clinic eight weeks after discharge.

note:
Telehealth video visit, geriatrics follow-up, for a 65-year-old male with urinary incontinence. His daughter, who lives with him and helps with his medications, joined the call and provided part of the history. The visit was done by secure video with the patient at home in a private room.

The patient reports leaking urine for about four months. He feels a sudden strong urge to urinate and often cannot reach the bathroom in time, with leakage of a moderate amount about three to four times a day. He is up two to three times a night to urinate. His daughter adds that he has had several wet nights and has stopped going to his weekly card game because of embarrassment. He denies burning with urination, blood in the urine, and fever. He denies leakage when coughing or lifting. He denies back pain, new leg weakness, and numbness. His daughter reports no recent confusion and no falls.

Past history includes benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension. Current medications are tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily, which his daughter says he usually takes in the late afternoon. He drinks about three cups of coffee a day, mostly after lunch.

Home readings reported by the patient this morning were blood pressure 134/80 and heart rate 72 on his home cuff. A urinalysis done at an outside lab last week was negative for leukocyte esterase, nitrite, and blood.

On limited video examination he appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, and is alert and oriented. He walks steadily to the bathroom door when asked. There is no visible swelling of the face or legs. The abdominal and genital examination could not be performed by video.

Impression is urge-predominant urinary incontinence with nocturia, most consistent with overactive bladder, in a man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and well-controlled hypertension. There is no evidence of infection on the urinalysis.

I will start mirabegron 25 mg once daily rather than an anticholinergic to avoid anticholinergic side effects. Tamsulosin continues unchanged. Hydrochlorothiazide will be moved to the morning to reduce nighttime urination. He should cut back on caffeine, stop drinking fluids two hours before bed, and keep a three-day bladder diary. He will return for an in-person visit in 4 weeks for a bladder scan for post-void residual and a blood pressure check, since mirabegron can raise blood pressure. Return precautions were reviewed, including inability to pass urine or severe lower abdominal pain.
summary: A 65-year-old male with benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension was seen by video for about four months of urgency-related urine leakage and nocturia, with his daughter providing part of the history. He denies burning with urination, blood in the urine and fever, home blood pressure was 134/80, and a urinalysis last week was negative for infection. The impression is urge-predominant urinary incontinence, most consistent with overactive bladder. Mirabegron 25 mg once daily was started, tamsulosin continues, hydrochlorothiazide will be moved to the morning, and he will have an in-person visit in 4 weeks with a bladder scan.

note:
Follow-up visit in the psychiatry specialty clinic for a 49-year-old male with schizophrenia who has been stable for several years on a long-acting injectable antipsychotic. He receives paliperidone palmitate 156 mg intramuscularly every 4 weeks, and his last injection was about five weeks ago, so he is one week overdue. He explained that the copay for the injection and the clinic visit fee made him put off the appointment. Because of cost he has also been skipping doses of his metformin and splitting his atorvastatin tablets to make them last longer. He also has type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. His current medications are paliperidone palmitate 156 mg every 4 weeks, metformin 500 mg once daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly.

He says he is hearing no voices and denies command hallucinations, paranoid thoughts, and suicidal or homicidal thoughts. His sleep is fair at about six hours a night and his appetite is good. He lives alone, attends a day program three days a week, and has not been hospitalized in more than five years.

On mental status examination he is casually dressed, cooperative, and makes good eye contact. Speech is normal in rate and volume, mood is described as okay, and affect is mildly constricted but appropriate. Thought process is linear, and there is no evidence of delusions or of responding to internal stimuli. Insight and judgment are fair. No tremor, rigidity, or abnormal movements are seen. Blood pressure is 128/82, heart rate 78, and weight 94 kg. Hemoglobin A1c today is 7.4%, up from 6.9% six months ago.

Impression is schizophrenia, currently stable but at risk of relapse because of the delayed injection and cost-related nonadherence, along with type 2 diabetes with slightly worse control after skipped metformin doses and hyperlipidemia. I gave paliperidone palmitate 156 mg intramuscularly today, and the next injection is due in 4 weeks. Metformin will be increased to 500 mg twice daily. I will continue atorvastatin 40 mg nightly and prescribe a 90-day supply. Social work and the clinic financial counselor will help him apply for a patient assistance program for the injection and give him a low-cost generic pharmacy list. A lipid panel will be checked at the next visit and hemoglobin A1c repeated in 3 months. He agrees to call the clinic if cost prevents him from taking any medication or keeping an appointment. He will return in 4 weeks.

He denies voices, command hallucinations, paranoid thoughts and suicidal or homicidal thoughts, and examination showed no psychosis or abnormal movements, with hemoglobin A1c up to 7.4%. The impression is stable schizophrenia at risk of relapse, with type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. Paliperidone palmitate 156 mg was given, metformin was increased to 500 mg twice daily, and social work will help with a patient assistance program.

note:
Hospital medicine progress note, hospital day 2, dictating on a 44-year-old female admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. She presented two days ago with three days of black tarry stools and one episode of coffee ground emesis, along with lightheadedness on standing. She denies chest pain, denies shortness of breath at rest, denies abdominal distension, and denies any bright red blood per rectum. Past medical history includes a pulmonary embolism about eight months ago for which she takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily, hypertension on lisinopril 20 mg daily, type 2 diabetes on metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and chronic low back pain for which she had been taking ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for the past month. She is a current tobacco smoker at about one pack per day, correction, about half a pack per day, for twenty years. She denies alcohol use and has no known drug allergies.

On admission her hemoglobin was 7.4 compared with a baseline of 12.8 last year, and she received two units of packed red blood cells overnight with an appropriate rise. This morning her hemoglobin is 8.6, correction, 8.9. Platelets are 245, INR 1.3, creatinine 0.8, and BUN 28. Her last dose of apixaban was the evening before admission. She has been hemodynamically stable overnight with no further melena since admission. Vitals this morning are temperature 98.4 Fahrenheit, heart rate 88, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.

On examination she has conjunctival pallor and mild epigastric tenderness. Her rhythm is regular and the lungs are clear. She is in no acute distress. There is no guarding, no rebound, and no abdominal distension. Rectal exam in the emergency department showed melena.

Upper endoscopy yesterday afternoon showed a 1.5 cm gastric antral ulcer with a visible vessel, which was treated with epinephrine injection and two hemoclips, and biopsies were taken to test for H. pylori. She was started on pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus followed by an infusion at 8 mg per hour, which I am changing today to pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily.

Assessment and plan by problem. Number one, upper gastrointestinal bleed from an NSAID-associated gastric ulcer, status post endoscopic therapy and hemodynamically stable. I am continuing the PPI as above and permanently stopping ibuprofen and all other NSAIDs. We will follow the H. pylori pathology and treat if positive. I advanced her to a full liquid diet today and will repeat a CBC every 8 hours today. Number two, acute blood loss anemia, status post transfusion, goal hemoglobin above 7, and I will add iron studies. Number three, history of pulmonary embolism on apixaban, which has been held since admission. Given the high-risk bleed I will keep apixaban held and plan to restart in about 7 days if the hemoglobin stays stable, after confirming with GI and pharmacy, with no heparin bridging. Number four, hypertension, lisinopril is on hold while she is at risk of hypovolemia and her pressure is acceptable. Number five, type 2 diabetes, metformin is held in the hospital and I started insulin lispro correction scale with meals, hemoglobin A1c is 7.9%. Number six, tobacco use, I counseled her on cessation and started a nicotine patch 14 mg daily. Number seven, chronic low back pain, I started acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed and she will see her primary care clinician after discharge for non-NSAID options. Anticipate discharge in two days if hemoglobin remains stable.
summary: A 44-year-old female on apixaban for a prior pulmonary embolism was admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed after a month of ibuprofen use, with black tarry stools, coffee ground emesis and a hemoglobin of 7.4. Endoscopy showed a 1.5 cm gastric antral ulcer with a visible vessel treated with epinephrine injection and hemoclips, and she received two units of packed red blood cells with hemoglobin rising to 8.9. The impression is an NSAID-associated gastric ulcer bleed with acute blood loss anemia, in a patient with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and ongoing tobacco use. Ibuprofen is stopped, apixaban and lisinopril are held, pantoprazole is changed to 40 mg IV twice daily, and discharge is anticipated in two days.

note:
Doctor: Hi, I'm the emergency physician. I have you down as a 34-year-old female with severe right-sided pain, is that right?
Patient: Yes. It started this morning in my back on the right side and it comes in waves. It goes down toward my groin, and I threw up twice.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever and no chills.
Doctor: Any burning when you pee, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No burning, but my urine looked pink this morning.
Doctor: Have you ever had a kidney stone before?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any medical problems, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have high blood pressure and I take lisinopril 10 mg every day.
Doctor: Any allergies to medications?
Patient: Yes, I'm allergic to ibuprofen. I get hives and my lips swell up.
Doctor: Thank you, that's important. I will not give you ibuprofen, ketorolac, or any other anti-inflammatory pain medicine. Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
Patient: No, my period ended last week.
Doctor: Okay, we will still do a urine pregnancy test. Your vitals when you came in were blood pressure 148/90, heart rate 98, temperature 98.2, and oxygen saturation 99 percent on room air. You look uncomfortable. On exam your abdomen is soft with mild tenderness on the right, and you have right flank tenderness. There is no rebound and no guarding.
Patient: It hurts when you press on my back there.
Doctor: Your urinalysis shows blood but no signs of infection, and your pregnancy test is negative. The CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis shows a 5 mm stone in the right ureter with mild swelling of the kidney, which is called hydronephrosis. Your creatinine is 0.9, so your kidney function is normal.
Patient: Okay. Can I get something for the pain? I feel sick to my stomach too.
Doctor: Yes. I am going to give you acetaminophen 1000 mg by IV, ondansetron 4 mg IV for the nausea, and morphine 4 mg IV for the severe pain.
Patient: Thank you.
Doctor: My impression is a kidney stone causing renal colic. A 5 mm stone has a good chance of passing on its own. You will go home with tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day to help the stone pass and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for pain. Drink plenty of fluids and strain your urine. Please follow up with urology in one week. Come back right away for fever, pain you cannot control, or if you cannot keep fluids down.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: A 34-year-old female with high blood pressure presented to the emergency department with severe right-sided pain, vomiting and pink urine, and she is allergic to ibuprofen. Urinalysis showed blood without infection, the pregnancy test was negative, and CT showed a 5 mm right ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis and normal creatinine. The impression is a kidney stone causing renal colic. She received IV acetaminophen, ondansetron and morphine, and will go home on tamsulosin and acetaminophen with strained urine, fluids and urology follow-up in one week, while avoiding anti-inflammatory pain medicines.

soap.assessment: Kidney stone causing renal colic, with a 5 mm right ureteral stone and mild hydronephrosis; stone has a good chance of passing on its own.

note:
Geriatrics clinic dictation on a 93-year-old male seen for follow-up of mild cognitive impairment. He says he left school after the sixth grade and has trouble reading the labels on his pill bottles, so I used plain language, short sentences, and teach-back throughout the visit. He has noticed memory problems over about two years, including misplacing his glasses, repeating questions, and occasionally forgetting appointments. He still manages his own bathing, dressing, and meals. He denies getting lost in familiar places, denies falls, denies hallucinations, and denies feeling sad or hopeless. His sleep is poor and he takes diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime, which he has used for years. Past history includes hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine 10 mg daily, correction, 5 mg daily, as confirmed on the bottle he brought in.

Vitals today are blood pressure 142 over 78 and heart rate 68, and his weight is stable. On examination he is alert and cooperative and follows conversation well with his hearing aids in place. Heart and lungs are normal and his gait is slow but steady without a device. His score on the MoCA today was 22 out of 30, with losses mainly in delayed recall and attention. TSH from last month was normal at 2.1, and his vitamin B12 level was low at 190.

Impression is mild cognitive impairment, with possible contributions from the nightly diphenhydramine and low vitamin B12, along with insomnia and hypertension that is near goal.

Plan is as follows. I am stopping diphenhydramine because it is anticholinergic and can worsen memory, and I reviewed simple sleep habits with him. I am starting vitamin B12 1000 mcg daily by mouth. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. I ordered a non-contrast head CT. I gave him a large-print picture medication list and a weekly pill organizer, and I asked the home health nurse to set up his pills for the first month. Teach-back confirmed that he understands to stop the sleep pill and take one B12 tablet each day. Follow up in three months with a repeat B12 level, sooner if his memory worsens or he has a fall.
summary: A 93-year-old male with limited health literacy was seen for follow-up of mild cognitive impairment after about two years of memory problems. He denies falls, hallucinations and low mood, his MoCA score was 22 out of 30, TSH was normal and vitamin B12 was low at 190. The impression is mild cognitive impairment with possible contributions from nightly diphenhydramine and low vitamin B12, along with insomnia and hypertension near goal. Diphenhydramine was stopped, vitamin B12 1000 mcg daily was started, amlodipine 5 mg daily continues, a head CT was ordered, and home health will set up his pills.

note:
Telephone visit (audio only) for neurology follow-up of post-concussion syndrome in a 71-year-old male. Identity was confirmed and he agreed to be seen by phone.

He fell from a step stool at home about five weeks ago and struck his head without losing consciousness. He was seen in the emergency department, where a head CT was normal. Since then he has had daily headaches that are worse in the afternoon, dizziness when standing quickly, difficulty concentrating when reading, and sensitivity to bright light. He sleeps poorly and wakes twice a night. His symptoms are slowly improving but have not resolved. He denies vomiting, denies new weakness or numbness, denies double vision, and denies confusion. He has no history of seizures and no other chronic medical conditions. He takes acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for headache, about four days a week.

No home vital signs were available. No physical examination could be done by phone. His speech was fluent and clear, he answered questions appropriately, and there was no word-finding difficulty.

Impression is post-concussion syndrome, improving, with no red-flag symptoms. I advised him to limit acetaminophen to three days a week to avoid rebound headaches and to continue 500 mg as needed on those days. He should return gradually to reading and other mental activity with frequent breaks, limit screen time, keep a regular sleep schedule, and avoid driving while dizzy. I also advised him to use a stable ladder or have someone nearby when reaching up high. We will speak again by phone in four weeks. He should seek in-person care promptly for a worsening headache, repeated emesis, weakness on one side, or new disorientation. If symptoms have not resolved by three months, we will consider vestibular therapy.
summary: A 71-year-old male was seen by telephone for post-concussion syndrome about five weeks after a fall from a step stool with a head strike and a normal head CT. He has daily headaches, dizziness when standing quickly, difficulty concentrating and sensitivity to bright light, but denies vomiting, new weakness or numbness, double vision and confusion. The impression is improving post-concussion syndrome without red-flag symptoms. He was advised to limit acetaminophen to three days a week, return gradually to mental activity, and have a phone follow-up in four weeks, with vestibular therapy considered if symptoms persist at three months.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. Your referral says you're a 28-year-old female with a cough that won't go away. Tell me about it.
Patient: It's been about three months. It's a dry cough, mostly at night and first thing in the morning. I also feel like there's mucus dripping down the back of my throat, and I clear my throat all the time.
Doctor: Any wheezing or shortness of breath?
Patient: No wheezing, and I can exercise fine. No shortness of breath.
Doctor: Any fever, coughing up blood, or weight loss?
Patient: No, none of that.
Doctor: Do you smoke, or have heartburn or a sour taste in your mouth?
Patient: I've never smoked, and no heartburn or sour taste. I do have a stuffy nose most of the year, and I take cetirizine 10 mg at night when it's bad.
Doctor: Okay. Do you take any blood pressure pills?
Patient: No, I don't take any other medicines.
Doctor: Good, that rules out a medication cough. On exam your lungs are clear with no wheezing, and your oxygen level is normal. Your nose is swollen inside with clear mucus, and the back of your throat has a cobblestone look. Your chest X-ray today is clear and your spirometry is normal.
Patient: So what's causing the cough?
Doctor: I think this is chronic cough from upper airway cough syndrome, which is post-nasal drip from allergic rhinitis. I'm starting fluticasone nasal spray, two sprays in each nostril once daily. Keep taking cetirizine 10 mg at night. I'd like to see you in six weeks, and if the cough is not better we will test for asthma and reflux.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good. Thank you.
summary: A 28-year-old female was seen for a dry cough of about three months, worse at night and in the morning, with a sensation of mucus dripping down the back of her throat and a stuffy nose most of the year. note:
Telehealth video visit, gastroenterology, conducted on a secure video platform with a professional Spanish interpreter on the call for the entire visit. The patient is a 54-year-old female referred by her primary care clinician to discuss colorectal cancer screening. She is at home in a quiet room.

She has never had a colonoscopy or any stool-based screening test. She appeared anxious and asked many questions, including how painful the preparation is, whether the sedation is safe, what could go wrong, what happens if a polyp is found, how much it costs, and whether a stool test is just as good. Each question was answered through the interpreter. She is worried because a relative had colon cancer; she first said her sister had it at age 60, then clarified that it was her maternal aunt, and that she has no first-degree relatives with colorectal cancer.

She denies rectal bleeding, black stools, abdominal pain, unintentional weight loss, and any change in bowel habits. She reports occasional mild constipation that responds to fluids.

Past history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, GERD, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications by her report are metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. On reviewing the bottles by video she corrected the metformin: it is metformin ER 1000 mg once daily, not 500 mg twice daily. She has also been taking over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg for knee pain, about three times a week, and has had more heartburn recently. She takes no blood thinners. She has no known drug allergies.

Home readings this morning were blood pressure 130/82, heart rate 74, and fingerstick glucose 118, and her home scale weight was 78 kg. Results she had on hand from her primary care clinic show hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, LDL 142 mg/dL, and hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL two months ago.

On video she looked anxious but in no distress. She spoke in full sentences, had no visible jaundice or pallor, and moved comfortably. She pressed on her abdomen herself and reported no tenderness. A hands-on abdominal exam could not be done by video.

Impression is that she is at average risk for colorectal cancer with no alarm symptoms. I reviewed three options: colonoscopy every 10 years if normal, which also allows polyps to be removed during the same procedure; annual FIT; or a multi-target stool DNA test every 3 years. I explained that any positive stool test would still need a colonoscopy. After a long discussion she chose colonoscopy.

Plan is to schedule a screening colonoscopy in 4 to 6 weeks with sedation by an anesthesia team. She will use a split-dose polyethylene glycol bowel preparation, with written instructions in Spanish and teach-back through the interpreter. For her diabetes she should hold the metformin the morning of the procedure and check her glucose while on clear liquids. A nurse will call before the procedure to answer questions. Naproxen is stopped now because of the heartburn and the bleeding risk with polyp removal, and she can use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for knee pain instead. Omeprazole is increased from 20 mg to 40 mg daily for 8 weeks. Her other medications continue unchanged. She needs an adult to drive her home after the procedure. She should call for heavy bleeding from the rectum, tarry stools, or severe belly pain.

She denies rectal bleeding, black stools, abdominal pain, unintentional weight loss and change in bowel habits, and she has more heartburn from over-the-counter naproxen. The impression is average risk for colorectal cancer with no alarm symptoms, and after reviewing colonoscopy, FIT and stool DNA testing she chose colonoscopy. Naproxen is stopped, omeprazole is increased to 40 mg daily, and a split-dose bowel preparation with diabetes instructions was planned.

note:
Nephrology consultation. Requesting service is hospital medicine. Reason for consult is volume overload in a patient on maintenance hemodialysis.

HPI: This is a 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease from diabetic nephropathy on in-center hemodialysis three times weekly through a left arm arteriovenous fistula. He was admitted last night with shortness of breath and leg swelling. He returned about ten days ago from a three-week trip abroad, during which he completed only two dialysis sessions, and he admits to eating salty restaurant meals and drinking more fluids than usual. He estimates he has gained about 6 kg above his dry weight. He reports orthopnea and ankle swelling. He denies chest pain, fever, diarrhea, and cough. He still makes a small amount of urine.

Past history: end-stage renal disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Home medications are amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and sevelamer carbonate 800 mg three times daily with meals. No known drug allergies.

Exam: blood pressure 168/94, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 91% on 2 L nasal cannula, temperature 98.6 F. Elevated JVP, bibasilar crackles, and 2+ pitting edema to the knees. The fistula has a palpable thrill and audible bruit. There is no pericardial rub.

Data: potassium 5.8, sodium 134, hemoglobin 9.6. Chest x-ray shows pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. ECG shows sinus rhythm without peaked T waves. Hepatitis B surface antigen was negative at the dialysis unit last month.

Impression: Volume overload from missed dialysis sessions and dietary sodium and fluid excess in end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. Mild hyperkalemia. Hypertension, likely volume-mediated.

Recommendations: Urgent hemodialysis tonight with an ultrafiltration goal of 3 to 4 liters as tolerated and a 2 potassium bath. Daily dialysis until he reaches his dry weight. Hold lisinopril while potassium is elevated. Continue amlodipine 10 mg daily and sevelamer carbonate 800 mg three times daily with meals. Strict intake and output, a low-salt diet, and a fluid restriction of 1 liter per day. Repeat BMP after dialysis. Supplemental oxygen to keep saturation above 92%. Given the recent international travel, recheck hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody per dialysis unit protocol and notify his outpatient unit before he returns. Social work to help arrange dialysis for future travel. We will follow daily.
